plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two rose curves plotted on separate polar grids, set side by side and labeled (a) and (b) beneath. Each grid is built from dotted concentric circles crossed by dotted radial spokes, with solid horizontal and vertical axes arrowed at all four ends. Panel (a) holds a teal curve of eight identical petals, all springing from the origin at equal angular intervals so that four lie along the axes and four along the diagonals between them; its caption reads r = acos(n theta), n even. Panel (b) holds a curve in the same teal weight but with only three petals, one pointing straight down along the negative vertical axis and the other two angled up to the left and up to the right, spaced a third of a turn apart; its caption reads r = asin(n theta), n odd. Every petal reaches out to roughly the same radius, so each curve fills a circular envelope. Setting the panels side by side isolates the parity of n as the only thing governing the count: an even n produces 2n petals while an odd n produces just n, and the eight-petal and three-petal drawings are the two cases of that rule.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: For polar roses, the parity of n determines the number of petals: even n gives 2n petals, and odd n gives n petals.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Make the default state a clean static two-panel replica with no amplitude marker, endpoint circle, petal-count annotation, or extra labels. Use a large side-by-side layout with the two polar grids scaled to fill most of the available drawing area while leaving enough margin so all axis arrowheads and captions remain visible when the UI panel is docked. Keep both panels fully inside the canvas. Use thin gray dotted polar grids, black horizontal and vertical axes with arrowheads at both ends, and thick teal rose curves with no fill. The left panel should show an eight-petal cosine-style rose centered on the origin; the caption below it must read exactly '(a) r = a cos(nθ), n even'. The right panel should show a three-petal sine-style rose centered on the origin; the caption below it must read exactly '(b) r = a sin(nθ), n odd'. Place captions below the grids with sufficient vertical padding to avoid clipping. Explanatory overlays should appear only when selected: petal-count labels and subtle petal highlights in the petal-count view, and orientation guide lines only in the sine-versus-cosine view.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Button/state for integer n: the learner steps through n values, the polar curve redraws with n petals for odd n and 2n petals for even n, making the parity rule visible instead of memorized.

authoredContext:
The formulas that generate the graph of a rose curve are given by r=acosnθ and r=asinnθ where a≠0. If n is even, the curve has 2n petals. If n is odd, the curve has n petals. See the figure.

Graph of two rose curves side by side. (A) is r=acos(ntheta), where n is even. Eight petals extending from origin, equally spaced. (B) is r=asin(ntheta) where n is odd. Three petals extending from the origin, equally spaced.

interactions.label: Integer n
interactions.teaches: Odd n produces n petals, but even n produces 2n petals, so petal count comes from parity rather than from the formula being sine or cosine

interactions.label: Rose form
interactions.teaches: Switching between cosine and sine rotates the rose, but the petal-count rule stays tied to n

interactions.label: Amplitude a
interactions.teaches: The value of a sets the maximum radius of every petal, changing the size of the rose without changing how many petals it has

interactions.label: Custom polar rose
interactions.teaches: The rose shape comes directly from multiplying θ by n inside sine or cosine and scaling the resulting radius by a

demo_steps.title: Start with the even cosine rose
demo_steps.narration: With n = 4 in r = a cos(nθ), the curve has eight petals, not four. This is the even-n rule: an even n creates 2n petals.

demo_steps.title: Change only n to an odd value
demo_steps.narration: Set n = 3 and the rose now has three petals. The formula type has not changed; the petal count changes because n changed from even to odd.

demo_steps.title: Switch cosine to sine
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to r = a sin(nθ). The three-petal rose rotates to a new orientation, but it still has three petals because n is still odd.

demo_steps.title: Scale the rose with a
demo_steps.narration: Increase a and each petal reaches farther from the origin. The circular envelope grows, but the number and spacing of petals do not change.

demo_steps.title: Test the rule yourself
demo_steps.narration: Try other integer values of n or edit the equation directly. The graph should confirm that parity controls petal count, while sine/cosine controls orientation and a controls size.

plan.keyInsight: In a polar rose r = a cos(nθ) or r = a sin(nθ), n controls petal count by parity: odd n gives n petals, even n gives 2n petals.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the textbook look with two side-by-side polar grids on a white background, each using thin dotted concentric circles and radial spokes. Use solid black horizontal and vertical axes with arrowheads at all four ends. Draw rose curves in a thick teal stroke with no fill, all petals meeting at the origin and reaching a common circular envelope. The left reference panel should show an eight-petal cosine rose with petals on the axes and diagonals; the right reference panel should show a three-petal sine rose with one petal pointing downward and two angled upward. In the interactive focus, keep the same polar-grid style and update the teal curve, formula label, petal-count annotation, and radius marker as controls change.
